free_tier.stated: AuraDB Free, quoted from the quotas page: 'AuraDB Free: A perpetual free tier for learning, prototyping, and small projects' with Nodes '200,000', Relationships '400,000' and Storage '1GB'. Vendor support adds: 'after a period of 72 hours of inactivity, we will automatically pause it ... If the database remains paused for 30 days, it will be deleted by the system.'

record.interface_detail: inferred from the tooling the provider documents; not probed
record.chaining: 200,000 nodes and 400,000 relationships is a complete citation graph or a mid-sized knowledge graph, and Aura's Cypher is the same query language as the open-source server, so a graph built here moves to a rented container unchanged.

limits.value: 400,000 relationships caps a graph before the node count does for any connected dataset, because the average degree in a real graph is above 2; the 1 GB storage ceiling is the third constraint and usually arrives at the same time.

evidence.proved: 'AuraDB Free: A perpetual free tier for learning, prototyping, and small projects' with Nodes 200,000, Relationships 400,000, Storage 1GB, quoted
AuraDB Free is 'Starting at $0'; the plan table lists 'Auto-pause/resume' as included, backups 'Not Included' to 'On-demand', and 'Available Zone' as single-zone
'after a period of 72 hours of inactivity, we will automatically pause it ... If the database remains paused for 30 days, it will be deleted by the system', quoted

record.notes: Free instances run on GCP us-central1 only, cannot be paused by the user, and have on-demand backups only. A read-only query does not reset the 72-hour timer, because inactivity is defined as no updates or write queries, so a monitoring ping that only reads will not keep the graph awake. The graphacademy course page states the same limits.
